name: Metalcore
about: Metalcore is the point where hardcore punk's breakdowns and bark meet metal's riffs and technique. The first wave came out of the early-1990s hardcore scene: Integrity in Cleveland, Earth Crisis in Syracuse, Cave In in Boston, Hatebreed in Connecticut, thrashing like Slayer and moving like a mosh pit. By the end of the decade Botch and Converge had pushed it toward chaos, and Converge's Jane Doe in 2001 became its defining record. A second wave took the Gothenburg melodic death metal of At the Gates and In Flames, added clean-sung choruses and breakdowns, and sold millions: Killswitch Engage, As I Lay Dying, Unearth, Avenged Sevenfold. Since the 2010s it has split between arena-sized acts like Architects and Bring Me the Horizon and a hardcore underground led by Code Orange and Knocked Loose.

artists.name: Hatebreed
artists.why: the breakdown as a way of life

albums.title: Jane Doe
albums.why: Jacob Bannon's break-up howl and Kurt Ballou's whiplash riffing on the record that made chaos, grief and hardcore into high art, and metalcore's one true landmark.

albums.title: Systems Overload
albums.why: Dwid Hellion's occult rage and Slayer-schooled riffs on the Cleveland band's second album, the holy-terror blueprint every heavy hardcore band still consults.

albums.title: We Are the Romans
albums.why: Tacoma's quartet made a jagged, intelligent and surprisingly melodic record that drew the line between metalcore and the mathcore that followed.

albums.title: Alive or Just Breathing
albums.why: Adam Dutkiewicz's production, Jesse Leach's clean choruses and My Last Serenade set the template for the entire melodic-metalcore boom.

albums.title: Destroy the Machines
albums.why: Vegan straight-edge militancy delivered over downtuned, metallic riffs, the Syracuse band's debut gave 1990s hardcore its heaviest ideology.

albums.title: Fixation on a Co-Worker
albums.why: The New Jersey band's only album is a nasty, dissonant workplace nightmare that seeded the noisier side of metalcore.

albums.title: Petitioning the Empty Sky
albums.why: Before Jane Doe, Converge's first proper album already had the frantic tempo shifts and Bannon's shriek, if not yet the focus.

albums.title: Satisfaction Is the Death of Desire
albums.why: Jamey Jasta's motivational bellow and a relentless parade of breakdowns made the Connecticut band's debut the sound of every pit for a decade.

albums.title: Hearts Once Nourished with Hope and Compassion
albums.why: The Florida band's debut fused hardcore with melodic, almost progressive guitar lines, the seed of melodic metalcore before Gothenburg arrived.

albums.title: Where Blood and Fire Bring Rest
albums.why: Dan Weyandt's shredded scream and bleak, spiritual lyrics over sludgy riffs made the Pennsylvania band's third album Christian metalcore's finest hour.

albums.title: Until Your Heart Stops
albums.why: Boston teenagers playing dizzying, technical metalcore with space-rock interludes, before they turned toward Radiohead and Jupiter.

albums.title: The Opposite of December
albums.why: Screamed verses, sung choruses and genuine melody from Miami, the album that made metalcore emotional and pointed at the 2000s mainstream.

albums.title: Waking the Fallen
albums.why: Twin-guitar harmonies, M. Shadows's screams and clean singing, and an Iron Maiden-sized ambition that soon carried the band out of the genre.

albums.title: Hot Damn!
albums.why: Keith Buckley's literary wit and the Buckley brothers' swinging, Southern-rock-inflected riffs made the Buffalo band's second album a genre favorite.

albums.title: The Oncoming Storm
albums.why: Boston's Unearth turned At the Gates riffs and breakdowns into a tight, thrashing record that defined the Metal Blade wing of the boom.

albums.title: The End of Heartache
albums.why: Howard Jones's soulful voice replaced Leach's and the title track went to radio, the band's commercial peak and a Grammy nominee.

albums.title: Of Malice and the Magnum Heart
albums.why: Devin Townsend produced the Milwaukee band's debut, written after a fatal van crash, into something unusually melodic, mournful and precise.

albums.title: Define the Great Line
albums.why: Spencer Chamberlain's screams and Aaron Gillespie's choruses on a darker, post-metal-tinged album that debuted at number two.

albums.title: An Ocean Between Us
albums.why: The San Diego band's most polished and thrash-heavy album, with Nothing Left and The Sound of Truth its arena-ready peaks.

albums.title: Constellations
albums.why: Technical, rhythmically inventive Christian metalcore from Pennsylvania, with Matt Greiner's drumming its secret weapon.

albums.title: Sempiternal
albums.why: Oli Sykes's Sheffield band traded deathcore for electronics, melody and stadium ambition on the album that made them Britain's biggest heavy act.

albums.title: Lost Forever // Lost Together
albums.why: Tom Searle's politically charged riffs and Sam Carter's scream on the record that turned the Brighton band from cult favorites into festival headliners.

albums.title: Forever
albums.why: Pittsburgh's Code Orange added industrial noise, glitches and nu-metal bounce to hardcore on a Grammy-nominated album that reset the underground.

albums.title: A Different Shade of Blue
albums.why: Bryan Garris's piercing shriek and the Kentucky band's death-metal-tinged breakdowns made the heaviest hardcore record of its decade a genuine hit.
